title: Using LP2 as a key for the 256-byte payload
question: Can the unsolved LP2 rune stream decode the 256-byte payload from pages 49–51 when the running key may skip positions?
reader_question: Can the manuscript itself unlock the payload from pages 49–51?
summary: Adds the previously skipped pages 49–51 payload to the LP2-as-key search. No tested setting produces a qualifying reading, but a known-message check shows why this cannot rule out the method.
finding: All eight payload labels return complete 256-rune outputs; none passes the −5.5 source score bar. The best source-selected score is −7.090111. Seven of eight 256-rune plants recover exactly; reversed-key/+ recovers 253/256 despite a higher score than the retained true path. Original source 80% character gate passes. Combined 48-label selection has no source hit.
reader_finding: None of the eight settings reached the English-score threshold. In a separate check, the search preferred three wrong runes over the known answer. This result does not rule out using LP2 as a key.
limitations: No historical payload.bin identification, other payloads, offsets, encodings, key/skip models, repaired AN END bytes, full-search significance, plaintext confirmation or power-validated model exclusion. Only the best new source case receives a separate post-target normalized terminal-beam audit. The supplied canon_256 input is an amendment, not recovery of the unavailable historical payload.bin. The stronger exact-recovery gate failed before target decoding; the dated amendment authorizes diagnostic source completion only. The source chooses by cumulative score but reports a normalized score.
reader_limit: Only the stated payload and key-skipping rules were tested. Its bytes come from a preserved canonical file; the missing historical input was not recovered.
next_steps: A separate preregistered study would need a decoder whose recovery criterion is validated for its intended claim; retain these failed controls rather than treating target score failure as rejection.
